topic: Agent complexity, not autonomy, is the risk
angle: The real failure mode is the messy web between agents, not any single bot.
sourceTitle: Enterprise AI's real risk isn't autonomous agents. It's the complexity between them.
linkedinPost:
Enterprises aren’t deploying a “super-agent.” They’re stitching together a flock of bots that call each other, tap old systems, and rack up costs in the shadows.

A recent piece from VentureBeat argues the real risk in enterprise AI isn’t autonomy—it’s the complexity between agents. That maps exactly to what I see on the ground.

In production, failure looks like circular handoffs, orphaned API calls, and surprise bills from retries. No one designed the “between.”

My playbook: start with one narrowly scoped agent and draw the dependency graph like a wiring diagram. Add timeouts, idempotency, and a hard kill switch. Put observability on inter-agent calls first, not last.

Create a simple “service catalog” for agents: owner, inputs, outputs, SLOs. Give each agent a budget (latency, cost), and fail closed if another bot exceeds it. Measure task success rate, MTTR, and “control breaches” (actions outside contract).

If you can’t trace a decision across agents end-to-end, you don’t have value—you have risk with a nice demo.

Where in your stack does the “between” live today—and who owns it? #EnterpriseAI #AIStrategy #AIAdoption #AITransformation
xPost: The risk in enterprise AI isn’t a rogue super-bot. It’s the messy web between dozens of agents. Map the “between,” set budgets, add kill switches, and observe inter-agent calls first—not last. Ownership beats hype. #EnterpriseAI #AIStrategy
